questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.sub_topic: Temple meant for the royal household
questions.question: Which temple in Vijayanagara's royal centre, decorated with sculpted panels of the Ramayana, was probably meant to be used only by the king and his family?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The Hazara Rama temple
Why: The Hazara Rama temple in the royal centre was probably meant for the king and his family. Its walls carry panels from the Ramayana.
Why not the others: (A) Virupaksha and (B) Vitthala are in the sacred centre and were open to wider worship. (D) Pampadevi is linked with the local goddess.
Key point: The royal centre had over sixty temples, showing how closely rulers linked themselves with the gods.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.question: Al-Biruni's *Kitab-ul-Hind* is written in a simple, lucid style. It is divided into ____ chapters on subjects such as religion, philosophy, festivals and astronomy.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 80
Why: The *Kitab-ul-Hind* has 80 chapters. Each usually begins with a question, followed by a description based on Sanskrit traditions and a comparison with other cultures.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are the wrong number.
Key point: Al-Biruni's careful, structured method makes his work valuable despite his reliance on Brahmanical texts.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question: According to the *Manusmriti*, the wealth that a woman received as gifts at her marriage, and over which she had ownership, was called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Stridhana
Why: Stridhana, "a woman's wealth", was the gifts she received at marriage. Her children could inherit it, but her husband had no claim to it.
Why not the others: (A) Agrahara was land granted to Brahmanas. (B) Kanyadana was the gift of a daughter in marriage. (C) A gotra was a lineage unit.
Key point: Most land, cattle and money were controlled by men, so stridhana did not give women equal economic power.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.sub_topic: Groups and their actions in Non-Cooperation
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Group)
(A) Hill tribes of northern Andhra
(B) Peasants of Kumaun
(C) Peasants of Awadh
(D) Students

List-II (Action during Non-Cooperation)
(I) Violated the forest laws
(II) Did not pay taxes
(III) Stopped going to schools and colleges run by the government
(IV) Refused to carry loads for colonial officials
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Why: Hill tribes in northern Andhra violated the forest laws (I). Kumaun peasants refused to carry loads for officials (IV). Peasants in Awadh did not pay taxes (II), and students left government schools (III).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the hill tribes and Kumaun. (C) swaps Kumaun and Awadh. (D) swaps Awadh and the students.
Key point: Non-Cooperation became a mass movement because different groups adapted it to their own grievances.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question: Identify the incorrectly matched pair of a saint and the tradition he belonged to:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Shankaradeva – Nayanar
Why: Shankaradeva was a Vaishnava saint of Assam in the late fifteenth century. The Nayanars were Tamil devotees of Shiva.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are correctly matched.
Key point: Shankaradeva stressed devotion to Vishnu and set up namghars, houses of recitation and prayer.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Benami
(B) Amla
(C) Mahal
(D) Jhum

List-II (Meaning)
(I) An officer of the zamindar who collected rent from the village
(II) A purchase made in another person's name, so the real buyer stayed hidden
(III) Shifting cultivation
(IV) A revenue estate, which could be a village or a group of villages
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: A benami purchase hid the real buyer (II). An amla was the zamindar's rent collector (I). A mahal was a revenue estate (IV), and jhum was shifting cultivation (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps benami and amla. (B) swaps amla and mahal. (C) swaps mahal and jhum.
Key point: Zamindars used benami purchases to keep control of estates put up for auction.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) The compilation of the Rigveda
(B) The growth of Mahayana Buddhism
(C) The Buddha preaches his teachings
(D) Ashoka distributes portions of the Buddha's relics to build stupas
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (C), (D), (B)
Why: The Rigveda was compiled c. 1500–1000 BCE. The Buddha preached in the sixth–fifth centuries BCE, and Ashoka ruled in the third century BCE. Mahayana grew around the first century CE.
Why not the others: (B) puts Ashoka before the Buddha. (C) puts the Buddha before the Rigveda. (D) puts the Mahayana before Ashoka.
Key point: Ashoka distributed portions of the relics to important towns and ordered stupas to be built over them.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Mahajanapada)
(A) Vajji
(B) Kosala
(C) Avanti
(D) Gandhara

List-II (Capital or main city)
(I) Ujjayini
(II) Taxila
(III) Vaishali
(IV) Shravasti
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Vaishali was the centre of the Vajji (III), Shravasti of Kosala (IV), Ujjayini of Avanti (I) and Taxila of Gandhara (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Vajji and Kosala. (B) swaps Kosala and Avanti. (D) swaps Avanti and Gandhara.
Key point: Each mahajanapada had a capital city, often fortified, and Brahmanas began composing Dharmasutras that set norms for rulers.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Mauryan empire:
(A) The *Arthashastra*, parts of which are probably by Kautilya or Chanakya, is a source for Mauryan history.
(B) The Ashokan inscriptions are the only source that tells us anything about the Mauryas.
(C) Pataliputra was the capital, and Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri were important provincial centres.
(D) Megasthenes came to the Mauryan court as an ambassador of a Kushana king.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A) and (C) only
Why: (A) and (C) follow NCERT. The *Arthashastra* is a source, and the empire had five major political centres.
Why not the others: (B) is false. Other sources include Megasthenes, the *Arthashastra* and Buddhist, Jaina and Puranic texts. (D) is false. Megasthenes was the ambassador of Seleucus Nicator, a Greek ruler. Options (A), (C) and (D) each include a false statement.
Key point: The empire was not uniform. Control was strongest around the capital and the provincial centres.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) Bahadur Shah Zafar dies in Rangoon
(B) The British recapture Delhi
(C) The sepoys at Meerut break into mutiny
(D) Rani Lakshmi Bai dies fighting the British
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (B), (D), (A)
Why: The Meerut mutiny was in May 1857 and Delhi was recaptured in September 1857. Rani Lakshmi Bai died in June 1858, and Bahadur Shah Zafar died in Rangoon in November 1862.
Why not the others: (A) puts the Rani's death before Delhi's recapture. (B) puts Delhi's recapture before Meerut. (D) puts Bahadur Shah's death before the Rani's.
Key point: The British recaptured Delhi first, because it was the symbolic centre of the revolt.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Archaeologist)
(A) Alexander Cunningham
(B) John Marshall
(C) R.E.M. Wheeler
(D) R.D. Banerji

List-II (Contribution)
(I) Found seals at Mohenjodaro similar to those at Harappa
(II) As Director-General, announced the discovery of a new civilisation in 1924
(III) First Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India
(IV) Excavated by following the stratigraphy of the mound rather than uniform horizontal units
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: Cunningham was the first Director-General of the ASI (III). Marshall announced the new civilisation in 1924 (II). Wheeler followed the stratigraphy of the mound (IV), and Banerji found the Mohenjodaro seals (I).
Why not the others: (B) swaps Cunningham and Marshall. (C) swaps Marshall and Wheeler. (D) swaps Wheeler and Banerji.
Key point: Marshall dug in uniform horizontal units, which mixed up finds from different layers. Wheeler corrected this in the 1940s.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question: In the Mahabharata and Brahmanical texts, "patriliny" means:
options: A) Tracing descent from father to son, grandson and so on
B) Tracing descent through the mother's line, to her daughters
C) Marrying outside one's own kin group or village
D) A woman having several husbands at the same time
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Tracing descent from father to son, grandson and so on
Why: Patriliny traces descent from father to son and grandson. Most ruling families claimed to follow it.
Why not the others: (B) is matriliny, (C) is exogamy and (D) is polyandry.
Key point: Under patriliny, sons claimed the resources of their fathers, including the throne in the case of kings.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question: Which of the following was a strategy used to increase agricultural production between c. 600 BCE and 600 CE?
options: A) Using iron-tipped ploughshares in fertile alluvial areas
B) Using steam-powered pumps to lift water from wells
C) Growing tobacco and maize, newly brought from abroad
D) Using chemical fertilisers sold by state merchants
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Using iron-tipped ploughshares in fertile alluvial areas
Why: The iron-tipped ploughshare was used to turn fertile alluvial soil, as in the Ganga and Kaveri valleys. Transplantation of paddy and irrigation were other strategies.
Why not the others: (B) and (D) are modern. (C) Tobacco and maize came to India much later.
Key point: Higher production did not benefit everyone equally. Land grants and new landholders created sharper social differences.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.question: The word *chaitya* may have been derived from the word *chita*, which means:
options: C) An umbrella over the stupa
D) A railing around a shrine
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A funeral pyre
Why: Chaitya may come from chita, a funeral pyre, and so by extension a funerary mound.
Why not the others: (A) is a vihara. (C) is the chhatri. (D) is the railing (vedika).
Key point: Stupas were built over relics of the Buddha, such as bodily remains or objects he used.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question: Harappan weights were usually made of chert and were cubical, with no markings. The lower denominations of these weights were:
options: B) Based on the number twelve
D) Fixed by the size of the seal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Binary, such as 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16
Why: The lower denominations were binary (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and so on up to 12,800). The higher denominations followed the decimal system.
Why not the others: (A) Decimal applies to the higher denominations. (B) and (D) are not described in NCERT.
Key point: The smaller weights were probably used to weigh jewellery and beads, and some have been found at Mesopotamian sites too.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question: Krishnadeva Raya, under whom the Vijayanagara empire reached its peak, belonged to the ____ dynasty.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Tuluva
Why: Krishnadeva Raya belonged to the Tuluva dynasty.
Why not the others: (B) The Sangamas were the first dynasty, (C) the Saluvas came next, and (D) the Aravidu ruled after the Tuluvas.
Key point: Krishnadeva Raya's reign saw expansion, the building of temples and gopurams, and the founding of a suburb named after his mother.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi first forged the techniques of non-violent protest known as satyagraha in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) South Africa
Why: Gandhi developed satyagraha in South Africa, where he spent two decades and led campaigns against racial discrimination.
Why not the others: (A) Champaran and (C) Kheda came after his return to India. (B) He studied law in England.
Key point: In South Africa Gandhi also first brought together people of different religions in one struggle.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.question: In the Bombay Deccan, the moneylender, who was often also a trader, was called the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Sahukar
Why: The sahukar was the moneylender, often also a grain or cotton trader.
Why not the others: (A) A jotedar was a rich peasant in Bengal. (C) An amla was a zamindar's officer. (D) A patel was a village headman.
Key point: Ryots relied on sahukars for credit to pay their revenue, which led to growing debts.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Traveller)
(A) Ibn Battuta
(B) François Bernier
(C) Al-Biruni
(D) Jean-Baptiste Tavernier

List-II (Description)
(I) Wrote about the coconut and paan, which were unfamiliar to his readers
(II) A French jeweller who travelled to India at least six times
(III) Described a child widow made to commit sati at Lahore
(IV) Relied on Sanskrit texts to describe the caste system
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Ibn Battuta described the coconut and paan (I). Bernier described a child widow's sati at Lahore (III). Al-Biruni used Sanskrit texts to describe caste (IV), and Tavernier was a French jeweller (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Ibn Battuta and Bernier. (B) swaps Bernier and al-Biruni. (C) swaps al-Biruni and Tavernier.
Key point: Travellers described what was unfamiliar to their readers, so their accounts show both India and the traveller's own world.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.sub_topic: Rulers who first issued gold coins
questions.question: The first gold coins in the subcontinent were issued around the first century CE by the ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Kushanas
Why: NCERT says the Kushanas issued the first gold coins, around the first century CE. Their coins were similar in weight to those of Rome.
Why not the others: (A) The Mauryas used punch-marked coins. (B) The Guptas issued some of the most spectacular gold coins later. (C) The Satavahanas did not issue the first gold coins.
Key point: Gold coins were probably used for high-value transactions, such as long-distance trade.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.question: Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier into a respectable and educated family known for its expertise in Islamic religious law. Tangier lies in present-day:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Morocco
Why: Tangier is in Morocco. Ibn Battuta travelled widely before reaching Sind in 1333.
Why not the others: (B) Uzbekistan was al-Biruni's homeland (Khwarizm). (A) and (D) are lands he passed through, not his birthplace.
Key point: Ibn Battuta saw travel as a source of knowledge and experience, valued more than books.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question: Why did Gandhi make spinning on the charkha a central part of his programme?
options: A) Because spinning was the only way to pay the salt tax
B) Because the British had banned the charkha in 1920
C) Because the Congress constitution required all members to sell cloth
D) Because it stood for self-reliance and the dignity of manual labour
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Because it stood for self-reliance and the dignity of manual labour
Why: The charkha symbolised self-reliance and rejected machine-based modern civilisation. Gandhi wanted to break the boundary between mental and manual labour.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are false. (C) The Congress asked members to spin, not to sell cloth.
Key point: Gandhi often appeared in public with the charkha, and newspapers carried pictures of him spinning.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about how the British suppressed the revolt:
(A) A series of laws placed north India under martial law, and military officers and even ordinary Britons could try and punish suspected Indians.
(B) The ordinary processes of law and trial were kept fully in force throughout.
(C) In Awadh, the British tried to break the rebels' unity by promising big landholders that their estates would be returned.
(D) The British relied only on persuasion and avoided the use of military force.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) and (C) only
Why: (A) and (C) follow NCERT. Martial law gave sweeping powers, and landholders in Awadh were offered their estates back.
Why not the others: (B) is false, because ordinary law and trial were suspended and death was the punishment for rebellion. (D) is false, because the British used military force on a large scale. Options (B), (C) and (D) each include a false statement.
Key point: Repression and conciliation together broke the alliance between taluqdars and peasants in Awadh.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.sub_topic: Compilation of Kabir's verses in Rajasthan
questions.question: Kabir's verses are found in three distinct but overlapping traditions. The *Kabir Granthavali* is associated with:
options: B) The Adi Granth Sahib of the Sikhs
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The Dadupanth in Rajasthan
Why: The *Kabir Granthavali* is associated with the Dadupanth in Rajasthan.
Why not the others: (A) The *Bijak* is preserved by the Kabirpanth. (B) Many of his verses are in the Adi Granth, a separate tradition. (C) The Virashaivas followed Basavanna.
Key point: Since the verses come from different traditions, historians find it hard to know which ones Kabir himself composed.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.sub_topic: Meaning of jangli in Mughal sources
questions.question: In contemporary texts, the term *jangli* was used for forest dwellers. What did it really describe?
options: A) People who had no contact at all with settled villages, traders or rulers
B) People who lived by gathering forest produce, hunting and shifting cultivation
C) People who refused to pay any tax or tribute in any form to any ruler
D) People who lived only in towns but worked in the forests
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) People who lived by gathering forest produce, hunting and shifting cultivation
Why: Jangli did not mean the absence of civilisation. It described people who lived by gathering forest produce, hunting and shifting cultivation.
Why not the others: (A) Forest dwellers had contact with others through trade and as soldiers. (C) Many paid tribute in kind, such as elephants. (D) is a contradiction.
Key point: The state needed the forest for elephants, and forest products such as honey and gum were traded widely.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about slavery as Ibn Battuta described it:
(A) Slaves were openly sold in markets and were often given as gifts.
(B) The sultan employed female slaves to keep watch on his nobles.
(C) Slavery had been abolished in the Delhi Sultanate before he arrived.
(D) On reaching Sind, he bought horses, camels and slaves as gifts for the sultan.
Which of the statements given above is NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false. Ibn Battuta describes slavery as widespread, so it had certainly not been abolished.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Slaves were sold and gifted, female slaves watched the nobles, and Ibn Battuta himself bought slaves as gifts. Options (B), (C) and (D) all name a true statement as incorrect.
Key point: Slaves were used for domestic labour, and some, such as palanquin bearers, did the work of carrying people.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question: The *Manusmriti*, one of the best-known Dharmashastras, was compiled in Sanskrit between c. ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 200 BCE and 200 CE
Why: NCERT dates the *Manusmriti* to between c. 200 BCE and 200 CE.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are too early, and (D) is too late.
Key point: The Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras laid down norms for social life, but they were not followed by everyone.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Character)
(A) Ekalavya
(B) Drona
(C) Hidimba
(D) Draupadi

List-II (Description)
(I) A rakshasa woman who married Bhima
(II) A forest-dwelling nishada who gave up his thumb as a gift to his teacher
(III) A woman who married all five Pandavas
(IV) A Brahmana who taught archery to the Kuru princes
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Ekalavya, a nishada, cut off his thumb at Drona's demand (II). Drona taught archery to the Kuru princes (IV). Hidimba was a rakshasa woman who married Bhima (I), and Draupadi married the five Pandavas (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Ekalavya and Drona. (C) swaps Drona and Hidimba. (D) swaps Hidimba and Draupadi.
Key point: Ekalavya's story was told to show how social norms were enforced on those outside the Brahmanical order.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.sub_topic: Study of peasant images of Gandhi
questions.question: The historian who traced how peasants in Gorakhpur saw Gandhi through rumours of his miraculous powers was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Shahid Amin
Why: Shahid Amin studied how rumours about Gandhi spread among peasants in Gorakhpur in the early 1920s.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are other historians. None of them made this study.
Key point: Peasants saw Gandhi as a saviour who could end their misery, often beyond what he himself intended.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question: Harappan seals, the most distinctive artefact of the civilisation, were usually made of a stone called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Steatite
Why: Harappan seals were usually made of steatite, a soft stone. They often carry an animal motif and signs of the script.
Why not the others: (A) Lapis lazuli and (C) carnelian were used for beads. (D) Chert was used for weights.
Key point: Seals were pressed on clay to seal bags of goods, so an unbroken sealing showed the goods had not been tampered with.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.question: Identify the incorrectly matched pair of a term from early religious architecture and its meaning:
options: A) Shikhara – a tall structure above the central shrine
B) Vihara – a place where monks lived
C) Garbhagriha – a high gateway on the boundary of a temple
D) Chhatri – an umbrella-like structure on top of a stupa
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Garbhagriha – a high gateway on the boundary of a temple
Why: The garbhagriha was the small square room where the image of the main deity was placed. A high gateway is a gopuram.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are correctly matched.
Key point: Early temples were small and had one doorway for the worshipper to enter and offer worship.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question: The proclamations issued by rebel leaders in 1857, which called on people to join the fight against the British, were known as ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Ishtahars
Why: Rebel proclamations were called ishtahars, and many were issued in the name of Bahadur Shah Zafar.
Why not the others: (A) A firman was a royal order. (B) Fortnightly reports were later British official reports. (C) A fatwa is a legal opinion on Islamic law.
Key point: The ishtahars harked back to the pre-British world and listed the injustices of British rule.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about women in agrarian society in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries:
(A) Women in every community were denied any right to inherit property.
(B) Women sowed, weeded, threshed and winnowed the harvest.
(C) Women did artisanal tasks such as spinning yarn, sifting and kneading clay for pottery, and embroidery.
(D) Because women were valued as a labour force, bride-price rather than dowry was paid in many rural communities.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (C) and (D) only
Why: (B), (C) and (D) follow NCERT. Women worked in the fields and in crafts, and bride-price was common where their labour was valued.
Why not the others: (A) is false. Hindu and Muslim women did inherit property. Some Hindu widows sold their inherited land, and Muslim women had a share in inheritance. Option (B) leaves out the true statement (C), and options (A) and (D) include (A).
Key point: The value placed on women's labour did not end men's control over them, and high mortality made their child-bearing role important.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question: Small pots made of faience were possibly treated as precious at Harappan sites. Faience is a material made of:
options: A) Ground sand or silica, mixed with colour and gum, and then fired
B) Melted copper mixed with tin to make bronze
C) Shell cut from conch, as at sites on the coast
D) Clay moulded by hand and dried in the sun without firing
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Ground sand or silica, mixed with colour and gum, and then fired
Why: Faience is made of ground sand or silica mixed with colour and a gum, then fired. It was difficult to make, so faience objects may have been valued.
Why not the others: (B) describes bronze. (C) describes shell working. (D) describes sun-dried clay, not faience.
Key point: Archaeologists treat rare or difficult-to-make objects as possible signs of social difference.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Silsila
(B) Ziyarat
(C) Sama
(D) Murid

List-II (Meaning)
(I) Pilgrimage to the tomb of a Sufi saint
(II) A disciple of a Sufi master
(III) Mystical music, used to evoke divine ecstasy
(IV) A chain linking master and disciple in an unbroken line
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Why: A silsila is a chain linking master and disciple (IV). Ziyarat is pilgrimage to a saint's tomb (I). Sama is mystical music (III), and a murid is a disciple (II).
Why not the others: (B) swaps silsila and ziyarat. (C) swaps ziyarat and sama. (D) swaps sama and murid.
Key point: The silsila traced spiritual power back to the Prophet Muhammad through a line of masters.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) S.R. Rao begins excavations at Lothal
(B) Excavations begin at Mohenjodaro
(C) R.S. Bisht begins excavations at Dholavira
(D) Excavations begin at Harappa
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D), (B), (A), (C)
Why: Excavations began at Harappa in 1921 and at Mohenjodaro in 1925. S.R. Rao began work at Lothal in 1955, and R.S. Bisht at Dholavira in 1990.
Why not the others: (A) puts Lothal before Mohenjodaro. (B) puts Mohenjodaro before Harappa. (C) puts Dholavira before Lothal.
Key point: After Partition many major sites lay in Pakistan, so Indian archaeologists located new sites such as Lothal, Kalibangan and Dholavira.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about Vijayanagara's buildings:
(A) Krishnadeva Raya built the hall in front of the main shrine of the Virupaksha temple to mark his accession.
(B) The gopurams, or royal gateways, often dwarfed the towers on the central shrines.
(C) The deity of the Vitthala temple was a form of Shiva worshipped in Maharashtra.
(D) Inscriptions confirm that the Lotus Mahal was the king's council chamber.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A) and (B) only
Why: (A) and (B) follow NCERT. Krishnadeva Raya built the hall at the Virupaksha temple, and the gopurams towered over the shrines.
Why not the others: (C) is false, because Vitthala was a form of Vishnu worshipped in Maharashtra. (D) is false, because British travellers named the Lotus Mahal in the nineteenth century and its use is uncertain. Options (A), (B) and (C) each include a false statement.
Key point: Bringing Vitthala, a Maharashtrian deity, into the capital showed how the rulers drew on many regional traditions.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question: Early in 1857, reports from many parts of north India spoke of the mysterious distribution, from village to village, of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Chapatis
Why: Chapatis were passed from village to village. Nobody knew who was distributing them or why, and the British saw them as a sign of unrest.
Why not the others: (A) Greased cartridges were issued to sepoys, not passed between villages. (C) and (D) are not mentioned.
Key point: Rumours and prophecies spread in a society already anxious about British intentions.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.question: What did the East India Company hope to achieve by the Permanent Settlement of 1793?
options: A) A regular flow of revenue and a class of landholders keen to improve their land
B) The abolition of the zamindars and direct settlement with every ryot in Bengal
C) A sharp fall in the revenue paid to the Company in the first year
D) The handing over of all land in Bengal to the jotedars
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A regular flow of revenue and a class of landholders keen to improve their land
Why: The Company wanted a fixed, regular revenue and hoped that security of property would turn zamindars into improving landlords loyal to it.
Why not the others: (B) The settlement was made with zamindars, not ryots. (C) The demand was fixed high. (D) The jotedars were not the intended beneficiaries.
Key point: Fixing the revenue in perpetuity also meant the Company could not later share in rising agricultural income.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question: Vijayanagara rulers claimed to rule on behalf of the god Virupaksha. Their royal orders were usually signed, in Kannada script, as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) "Shri Virupaksha"
Why: Royal orders were signed "Shri Virupaksha", showing that the kings ruled on the god's behalf.
Why not the others: (B) was the name of one king. (C) "Hindu Suratrana" was a title the rulers took, meaning "Hindu sultan". (D) Pampadevi was a goddess.
Key point: The rulers' choice of the site was linked to local beliefs about Pampadevi and Virupaksha.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) The *Ain-i Akbari* is completed
(B) Aurangzeb dies
(C) Babur wins the battle of Panipat
(D) Akbar comes to the throne
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: Babur won at Panipat in 1526, Akbar became emperor in 1556, the *Ain* was completed in 1598, and Aurangzeb died in 1707.
Why not the others: (A) puts the *Ain* before Akbar's accession. (C) puts Akbar before Babur. (D) puts Aurangzeb's death before the *Ain*.
Key point: The *Ain-i Akbari* was the third volume of the *Akbar Nama* and the result of a major project of classification.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.sub_topic: The Buddha's teachings and the sangha
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about early Buddhism:
(A) The Buddha's foster mother, Mahapajapati Gotami, was the first woman to be ordained as a bhikkhuni.
(B) The Buddha taught that the world is transient (anicca) and soulless (anatta), and that sorrow (dukkha) is intrinsic to human existence.
(C) The Buddha allowed only those of high birth to join the sangha.
(D) Buddhism grew partly because it stressed conduct and values rather than claims of superiority based on birth.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) follow NCERT. Mahapajapati was the first bhikkhuni, the three teachings are as stated, and Buddhism's stress on conduct drew many people.
Why not the others: (C) is false. Members of the sangha were regarded as equal, and men and women from many social groups joined. Option (A) leaves out the true statement (D), and options (B) and (D) include (C).
Key point: Many bhikkhunis composed verses that were compiled in the Therigatha.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question: The local deity Jagannatha, "lord of the world", worshipped at Puri in Orissa, came to be identified as a form of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Vishnu
Why: By the twelfth century Jagannatha was identified with Vishnu, though the image kept its distinctive local form.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are other deities.
Key point: This shows how local cults were integrated into Puranic traditions, a process historians study closely.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.sub_topic: Revenue period in the Bombay Deccan
questions.question: In the Bombay Deccan, the revenue system introduced in the 1820s fixed the demand directly with the ryot after a survey of the soil, for a period of ____ years.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 30
Why: The revenue was fixed for 30 years, after which it was to be revised.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are the wrong period.
Key point: The first settlements had high demands, so many ryots fled their villages.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.question: Zamindars held extensive personal lands, cultivated for their own use by hired or servile labour. These lands were termed ____, meaning property.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Milkiyat
Why: Zamindars' personal lands were called milkiyat, meaning property. They could sell, bequeath or mortgage them.
Why not the others: (A) Jins-i kamil was a perfect crop. (B) Jama was the amount assessed and (C) hasil the amount collected.
Key point: Zamindars collected revenue for the state, which gave them control over other people's labour and produce.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.sub_topic: Member who pleaded for separate electorates
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

On 27 August 1947, B. Pocker Bahadur of Madras asked the Constituent Assembly to keep separate electorates. Minorities, he argued, exist in every country and cannot be wished away. They need a voice in the political life of the nation that is truly their own, and only a system in which they choose their own representatives can give them that voice.

Most nationalist members reacted sharply. They recalled that separate electorates had been brought in by the colonial government, and they blamed the system for the communal bitterness that had ended in Partition. Sardar Patel described it as a poison that had entered the body politic of the country.

Govind Ballabh Pant went further. He argued that the demand was not only harmful to the nation but suicidal for the minorities themselves. Separate electorates, he said, would isolate them permanently, stop them from winning the goodwill of others, and leave them without real influence in government. Citizens had to be built into one nation, not divided into separate compartments.

Separate electorates were rejected. By 1949 most Muslim members of the Assembly had also come to agree that the system worked against the interests of the minorities.

Question: According to the passage, the member who asked the Assembly to keep separate electorates in August 1947 was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) B. Pocker Bahadur
Why: The passage says that B. Pocker Bahadur of Madras asked the Assembly to keep separate electorates on 27 August 1947.
Why not the others: (A) Pant and (B) Patel opposed separate electorates. (D) Jaipal Singh spoke for the tribes and is not mentioned in the passage.
Key point: The debate on separate electorates was one of the most heated in the Assembly, because Partition had just taken place.

Separate electorates were rejected. By 1949 most Muslim members of the Assembly had also come to agree that the system worked against the interests of the minorities.

Question: What was the main reason Pocker Bahadur gave for keeping separate electorates?
options: A) Minorities needed a political voice of their own, which only their own representatives could give
B) Separate electorates would reduce the cost of holding elections across the provinces
C) The British government had promised to keep separate electorates after independence
D) The majority community had itself asked for separate electorates in every province
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Minorities needed a political voice of their own, which only their own representatives could give
Why: He argued that minorities need a voice "truly their own" in political life, which only a system of choosing their own representatives could provide.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are not arguments made in the passage.
Key point: Pocker Bahadur's case rested on the permanence of minorities and their need for meaningful representation.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: In the passage, Sardar Patel describes separate electorates as:
options: A) A necessary safeguard that should last for ten years
B) A system that should apply only to the princely states
C) A temporary measure until a national language was chosen
D) A poison that had entered the body politic of the country
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A poison that had entered the body politic of the country
Why: The passage says Patel described the system as a poison that had entered the body politic.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not views given in the passage, and none is Patel's.
Key point: For many nationalists, the memory of Partition made separate electorates seem a threat to national unity.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

On 27 August 1947, B. Pocker Bahadur of Madras asked the Constituent Assembly to keep separate electorates. Minorities, he argued, exist in every country and cannot be wished away. They need a voice in the political life of the nation that is truly their own, and only a system in which they choose their own representatives can give them that voice.

Most nationalist members reacted sharply. They recalled that separate electorates had been brought in by the colonial government, and they blamed the system for the communal bitterness that had ended in Partition. Sardar Patel described it as a poison that had entered the body politic of the country.

Govind Ballabh Pant went further. He argued that the demand was not only harmful to the nation but suicidal for the minorities themselves. Separate electorates, he said, would isolate them permanently, stop them from winning the goodwill of others, and leave them without real influence in government. Citizens had to be built into one nation, not divided into separate compartments.

Separate electorates were rejected. By 1949 most Muslim members of the Assembly had also come to agree that the system worked against the interests of the minorities.

Question: Why did Govind Ballabh Pant call the demand for separate electorates suicidal for the minorities?
options: A) Because the Constitution would ban minorities from contesting any election
B) Because the system would isolate the minorities permanently and leave them without real influence
C) Because separate electorates would force minorities to give up their languages
D) Because minorities would lose their right to vote in elections to the provincial legislatures
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Because the system would isolate the minorities permanently and leave them without real influence
Why: Pant argued that separate electorates would isolate the minorities permanently, stop them from winning the goodwill of others, and leave them without influence in government.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not in the passage. Minorities kept the vote and the right to contest under joint electorates.
Key point: Pant turned the argument round: a system meant to protect minorities would, he said, harm them most.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

On 27 August 1947, B. Pocker Bahadur of Madras asked the Constituent Assembly to keep separate electorates. Minorities, he argued, exist in every country and cannot be wished away. Citizens had to be built into one nation, not divided into separate compartments.

Separate electorates were rejected. By 1949 most Muslim members of the Assembly had also come to agree that the system worked against the interests of the minorities.

Question: Which of the following best explains why most members rejected separate electorates in 1947, as the passage presents it?
options: A) They believed minorities were too few in number to need any political representation at all
B) They wanted to give the princely states more seats in the central legislature than the provinces
C) They saw the system as a colonial device that had fed the communal bitterness behind Partition
D) They had been instructed by the British government to abolish separate electorates before independence
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) They saw the system as a colonial device that had fed the communal bitterness behind Partition
Why: The passage says nationalists recalled that the colonial government had brought in separate electorates, and blamed the system for the bitterness that ended in Partition.
Why not the others: (A) Members did not deny that minorities existed. Pant's concern was their future. (B) and (D) are not in the passage.
Key point: The rejection of separate electorates was shaped by the violence of 1946–47, as well as by arguments about citizenship.
